title: Foraging elderberries: harvest and safe preparation
subtitle: Cook before eating; raw elderberries cause nausea
excerpt: Elder produces its deep-purple fruit clusters in August and September along UK hedgerows. The berries cook into syrups, wine, and cordial. Raw elderberries cause nausea and vomiting; cooking deactivates the compound responsible.
sourceNotes: Richard Mabey, Food for Free (1972); John Wright, The Forager's Calendar (2019); BSBI species accounts for Sambucus nigra; Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.

glossaryTerms.definition: Matching three independent visual, scent, or habitat features before eating any wild plant. All three must match; a single mismatch means stop.
A wild plant that resembles an edible species closely enough to cause misidentification. Many look-alikes are toxic.
The specific habitat type where a wild plant grows, used as one of the three identification features.

content.text: Elder (Sambucus nigra) produces drooping clusters of deep-purple berries from August through September along UK hedgerows, woodland edges, and waste ground. The berries cook into syrups, wine, cordial, and fruit sauce. Do not eat raw elderberries: they contain a compound that causes nausea and vomiting in raw form and breaks down fully with heat. A minimum of ten minutes of simmering is enough. Verify your identification before eating; if in doubt, do not eat.
Apply the
rule-of-three identification
: confirm (1) the drooping cluster of many tiny deep-purple berries on red stalks, (2) the pinnate leaves with five to seven toothed leaflets in opposite pairs, and (3) the hedgerow or woodland-edge
foraging zone
. All three must match.
ID features
Berry cluster: drooping, flat-topped head of many small, round berries. Deep purple when ripe, with a purple-red juice. Green and red berries are under-ripe.
Stalks: red or purple, thin. The whole cluster droops under the weight of ripe fruit.
Leaves: pinnate, five to seven oval leaflets with toothed edges in opposite pairs along the stem. Crushed leaves smell unpleasant.
Bark: grey, corky, with white pith inside young stems.
Poisonous look-alikes
Two UK plants with dark berries can be confused with elderberry. Both are more dangerous than raw elderberry. These
look-alike plants
must be ruled out before picking.
Deadly nightshade (Atropa belladonna): shiny black berries singly or in pairs. Not in drooping clusters. Grows on a non-thorny herb, not a shrub with corky bark and pinnate leaves.
Dwarf elder (Sambucus ebulus): smaller plant, strongly unpleasant smell, berries upright rather than drooping. Toxic even when cooked. Rare in UK but found on waste ground.
When and how to harvest

Pick from late August through September when the berries are fully deep purple and the clusters droop under their weight. Cut the whole cluster stalk with secateurs rather than pulling individual berries. Take from several different elder plants and leave at least a third of the clusters for birds.
After harvesting

Strip the berries from the stalks with a fork into a colander and rinse under cold water. Cook before eating: simmer in a pan with water and sugar for a minimum of ten minutes for syrup. Use fresh juice, or ferment for wine. The berries freeze well on the stalks; strip them frozen.
Legal and ethical

The Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 and Theft Act 1968 allow collection of fruit from hedgerows and common land for personal use. Private land requires the landowner's permission. Leave at least a third of the clusters on every tree you visit for wildlife.

rows.cause: Berries eaten raw or insufficiently cooked
rows.fix: Seek medical advice if symptoms are severe. Always simmer elderberries for a minimum of ten minutes before consuming. Never eat them raw.

rows.symptom: Berry clusters are upright rather than drooping
rows.cause: The plant may be dwarf elder (Sambucus ebulus) rather than common elder
rows.fix: Do not harvest. Common elder berries droop when ripe; dwarf elder clusters point upward. Dwarf elder is toxic even when cooked.

rows.symptom: Berries are still green and red in September
rows.cause: Under-ripe; the season is running late or the location is cooler
rows.fix: Wait until the whole cluster is deep purple and the stalks turn red. Under-ripe berries are more irritating than ripe ones even after cooking.
